prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping, and for its development to systematic uncertainties near one part in 10^18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: one part, B059, Katori and Ye. The test I apply is whether we have found the original experiment and the people who did it. For the lattice clock the chain is short and documented. Katori's group proposed trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, where the light shift cancels between the clock states, and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock. This is the step that removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating very many atoms at once, and it is not a refinement of a comb or an ion clock. Ye's group then took the concept to its accuracy frontier, with coherence times, systematic control and many-body effects that brought uncertainties to about 1e-18. Those results have been reproduced and compared in independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE), and clock-to-clock comparisons and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements are routine. In response to the chair's first question, the distinction from 2005 and 2012 can be stated in the citation: the comb is the readout, the ion clock is a single-particle standard, and the lattice clock is a different physical scheme in which a many-atom ensemble is made insensitive to its own trap. I draw the line at the magic-wavelength lattice clock itself. Having read the full exchange, I see no competing configuration where the original-experiment question is answered as cleanly, so I stay with it.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I do not consider them closed. First, the committee must settle the Katori-Ye boundary against the primary record of 2003 to 2006. I am willing to credit Ye because his group made the lattice clock a 1e-18 instrument and the clock into a many-body system, but that is a development credit and the citation must say so. If the record showed that Ye's contribution is a later and better version of a result already complete, I would not support the second name. Second, Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow and Takamoto remain outside a two-name prize, and I do not want to dismiss them on the strength of agreement among our opening proposals, which is a statement about our shared sources and not independent verification. Third, the redefinition of the second is pending, so the societal payoff is still prospective. I treat it as a sign that the community regards the technology as ready, not as a requirement we must wait for, but a colleague who wants to wait for it has a fair argument. Finally, the 2005 and 2012 prizes make this the third precision-measurement prize in two decades, and that proximity is the chief risk.

responses.point: She says that seven of eight opening proposals give the same two names, so attribution is not in dispute, and that she does not regard Lemonde, Gill and Bloom as a reason for a third name.
responses.response: I agree that no third name is needed, but I would rest that on the record and not on the agreement among us. Eight members drawing on the same literature agreeing is weak evidence of who did the original work. What persuades me is that the proposal and first strontium demonstration are Katori's, and that the later work from Ye, SYRTE and others developed the same scheme. I also accept her point that the pending redefinition is a marker of maturity. Where we still differ is that I would write 'invention' and 'development' into the citation so that the credit is divided honestly between the two names, which her citation also does.

responses.point: He asks that the priority record be checked and notes that Ye's results build partly on the Hall-lineage comb and cavity-stabilisation work, and he flags that lineage as a possible recusal issue.
responses.response: This is the question the committee should answer, and I think it can answer it without depending on the comb. Ye's decisive lattice-clock results rest on the magic-wavelength scheme, the laser coherence and the control of systematics, and the comb is a tool he and everyone else uses to read the clock. That is why the citation must refer to the lattice clock and not to the comb or to optical clocks generally. I agree with his request for a primary-record check, and I would support asking outside reviewers to look at it, as the chair suggests. I also appreciate that he disclosed his Hall connection. In my view it is a reason to ask outside reviewers to verify Ye's contribution, not for him to leave the discussion.

responses.point: He moved from circuit QED to B059 and describes a clear division: proposal and first realisation on one side, the accuracy frontier and many-body physics on the other.
responses.response: We reach the same division from different directions, and I find it useful that a theorist embedded in experiments sees it too. I would add one caution. His phrase 'accuracy frontier' could be read as credit for a better measurement of something already done, which is the case I have said the prize should not cover. The defence is that the 1e-18 regime needed new physics, in the form of coherence across the ensemble, control of lattice and collisional shifts, and many-body clock physics, and not only refined engineering. I also note that his conflict statement concerns B013 and not B059, so his support for B059 is unaffected.

responses.point: He prefers IceCube (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) as a new observational window, with Spiering added because of the AMANDA/Baikal/DUMAND lineage, and lists B059 as an alternative.
responses.response: I share his weight on instruments that open new windows, and the diffuse flux is secure. His own round-1 statement identifies the issue that keeps me from joining him: the third name depends on a reading of who was decisive among the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lines, and he states that this comes from memory and is unverified. Halzen and Karle alone leave out the lineage that made the telescope credible, and adding Spiering is a judgement without a record behind it. Individual source associations are still at modest significance. I would rather revisit B043 in a later year when KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD have contributed independent checks and the attribution is documented.

responses.point: He prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, arguing that the phases are reproduced even though the pairing mechanism is open and that the prize would honour the phases and not the mechanism.
responses.response: I take his argument seriously and I rate this as the strongest condensed-matter case. I accept that the prize need not wait for a mechanism. My difficulty is attribution, and he states it himself: Yuan Cao was first author of the original experiments and is not among the three names, and Dean's hBN-encapsulated work is outside as well. A prize for the experimental discovery that names Jarillo-Herrero without Cao fails my test of 'the people who did the original work' unless the record shows Jarillo-Herrero as the decisive scientific leader. Eight years, sample dependence and twist-angle disorder also argue for patience. I keep B034 as my first alternative, and I would support it later if the credit question is settled.

responses.point: He prefers topological insulators (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) for the identified mechanism and fifteen years of independent confirmation, and concedes that the 2016 prize and the Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang claims are open.
responses.response: His maturity argument is the strongest in the room, and the HgTe experiment was one that could have failed and did not. I put B016 as an alternative for that reason. What keeps it behind B059 for me is credit. The 2016 prize already covers the topological foundation, and the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class has a prediction chain that includes Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for the HgTe route that Molenkamp's group tested, as well as Hasan's work on three dimensions. Within a three-name cap, each triple excludes someone with a documented claim, and I would not like to decide that on the information we have. The lattice clock does not carry that burden to the same extent.

responses.point: He prefers the Higgs discovery (Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee), calling the attribution problem one of drafting and stating that the Higgs has no prize for the particle itself.
responses.response: I agree that the discovery is secure and important, and I do not want to diminish it. But I cannot treat attribution as only a drafting question. The prize rewards 'the people doing the original work', and for a discovery by two collaborations of thousands, with Della Negra omitted from his own three, I cannot say that the names reflect scientific decisions and not collaboration roles. He and Pearce have both said that they cannot identify a defensible set. If the committee decided it could accept a collaboration prize and settled on a rule for the names, I would reconsider, but that decision must come first.

uncertainties: Whether the primary record of 2003 to 2006 shows that Katori's proposal and first demonstration are complete enough that Ye's role is a distinct development and not a later, more precise version.

Whether Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto or others have a claim that would make a two-name prize unfair, which I cannot settle from the discussion alone and which outside reviewers may need to check.
Whether the committee, after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, accepts the lattice clock as a distinct achievement and not a third precision-metrology prize.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be taken as a reason to wait; I lean to treat it as a sign of maturity, but I hold that view with moderate confidence.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I am an electron microscopist at Chalmers, so I would recuse myself from any decision on B027 (aberration-corrected TEM); it is not part of my final position and I do not propose it as a second part. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague, which does not bear on B059; his disclosed circuit QED ties concern B013 and not my preferred configuration. My earlier conflict on my opening top choice was a reason to change, and it does not apply to B059. From my profile I see no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the other contributors named in the clock record, and I note Kroll's Hall-lineage disclosure as a matter for the committee.
